lesson.title: Roman Numerals and Harmonic Function
lesson.summary: Roman numerals name each chord by its place in the key; tonic, predominant and dominant describe what the chord does.

section.title: Roman numeral analysis
section.p: A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree of its root. Its symbols add the rest of what you need to know:

list.li: Upper case for major triads (V), lower case for minor triads (ii).
A small circle for diminished (vii°), a plus sign for augmented (III+), and ø7 or °7 for half-diminished and diminished seventh chords.
Figures for the position: I6 and I6/4 for inverted triads, V7, V6/5, V4/3 and V4/2 for a seventh chord and its inversions.

section.p: The key comes first, followed by a colon: D: I. Many textbooks write major keys with an upper-case letter and minor keys with a lower-case letter. Some textbooks write every numeral in upper case and leave the quality to the key; this course uses the case to show the quality.

worked.title: Label a chord with a Roman numeral

step.p: Take this chord in D major. Read its notes from the bass up: E3, G3, C#4 and A4.
Stack the notes in thirds: A–C#–E–G. The root is A, the fifth degree of D major, and the chord is a dominant seventh chord: V7.
Find the position. The bass, E, is the fifth of the chord, so the chord is in second inversion. The full label is V4/3.

check.prompt: In F major, a chord has the notes A, C and F, with A in the bass. What is its Roman numeral?
check.explanation: The notes stack as F–A–C, the tonic triad of F major. The bass A is its third, so the triad is in first inversion: I6. The notes do not form iii, A–C–E.

check.prompt: In E minor, which Roman numeral names the chord B–D#–F#–A in root position?
check.explanation: B is the fifth degree of E minor. With the leading tone D# the triad is major and the seventh B–A minor, so the chord is the dominant seventh V7. With D instead of D# it would be the minor v7.

section.title: Three functions
section.p: Chords in a key do one of three jobs, called their harmonic function:

list.li: Tonic function: stability and rest. The tonic triad, I, is the home of the key; vi can stand in for it.
Predominant function: movement away from the tonic, towards the dominant. IV and ii are the main predominant chords; both contain the subdominant, degree 4.
Dominant function: tension that asks for the tonic. V and vii° contain the leading tone, which pulls up to the tonic.

section.p: The basic order of functions in a phrase is tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic. The predominant can be left out, but a dominant that leads back to the tonic is what makes the key clear.

figure.caption: Tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic in C major.
The same functions with ii6 as the predominant and V7 as the dominant.

section.p: The names vary: European textbooks following Hugo Riemann speak of tonic, subdominant and dominant functions, written T, S and D. Predominant, the common North American term, means the same as the subdominant function.
vii° and vii°7 share the leading tone and degree 4 with V7, so they act as dominants. iii is the weakest chord of the key; it most often moves to vi or IV.

check.prompt: Which function does ii6 normally have?
check.explanation: ii6 contains degree 4 in the bass and usually leads to V: it is a predominant chord, like IV. Tonic chords are I and vi; dominant chords are V and vii°.

check.prompt: Why can vii°6 take the place of V?
check.option: It contains the leading tone, which pulls up to the tonic
It contains the tonic, like I
It contains the subdominant, like IV
check.explanation: vii° shares two notes with V, degrees 7 and 2, including the leading tone. Together with degree 4 it forms the notes of V7 without the root, so it leads to I in the same way.

section.title: How chords follow each other
section.p: In common-practice music some chord successions are far more frequent than others. The strongest root movement is down a fifth (or up a fourth): V to I, ii to V, vi to ii. Chains of falling fifths lead from the tonic's most distant neighbours back to the tonic:

figure.caption: In C major, the roots A, D, G and C fall by fifths to the tonic.

section.p: A summary of the usual successions in major, following Kostka and Payne:

list.li: I can move to any chord.
vi moves to ii or IV.
ii and IV move to V or vii°; IV can also return to I.
V and vii° move to I; V can also move to vi.

section.p: Successions against this order, such as V to IV, are called retrogressions. They occur, but much less often. Minor keys follow the same pattern with their own chord qualities: i, ii°, III, iv, V, VI and vii°.

check.prompt: In a major key, which chord most often follows ii?
check.explanation: ii is a predominant chord: it leads to the dominant, and its root falls a fifth to the root of V. ii to vi or ii to I goes against the usual order.

step.p: Find the key. The key signature has two sharps, and the progression begins and ends with D–F#–A, so the key is D major, not B minor.
Take each chord in turn, collect its notes and stack them in thirds. The second chord, B–D–F#, is a minor triad on degree 6 with the root in the bass: vi.
The third chord has the notes G, E and B: in thirds, E–G–B, a minor triad on degree 2. The bass G is its third, so the chord is ii6.
The fourth chord, A–C#–E–G, is the dominant seventh chord on degree 5 with the root in the bass: V7. The last chord is I again.
Add the functions: I (tonic), vi (tonic, leading on), ii6 (predominant), V7 (dominant), I (tonic).

check.prompt: This progression is in G major. What is the Roman numeral of the highlighted chord?

figure.description: A grand staff with a key signature of one sharp and four four-part chords. The second chord is highlighted: its bass is in the second space of the bass staff.

check.explanation: The highlighted chord has the notes C, C, E and G: the triad C–E–G, built on degree 4 of G major, with the root in the bass. It is IV, a predominant chord between I and V.
